passages.text: STALACTITES, in natural history, stony bodies hanging from the roofs and sides of caverns, in the form of icicles.

They are formed by water, which, filtering through the rock above, carries with it particles of calcareous earth or spar; and the water, dropping slowly, leaves these particles behind, which harden into stone.
The drops which fall to the floor deposit the same matter there, and raise up stony cones or pillars called stalagmites; and these, meeting with the stalactites from above, often form entire columns.
Some of the older naturalists considered them as a kind of vegetation of stone, which grows from a seed like a plant, and draws its nourishment from the rock.
They grow so quickly in some caves, that a passage which was open within the memory of man is now closed up by them in a few years.
The most remarkable are those of the grotto of Antiparos in the Archipelago, and of Pool's Hole in Derbyshire.
A stalactite is a mineral formation that hangs from the ceiling of a cave or a similar place. The most common stalactites are speleothems, which form in limestone caves.

Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide and becomes weakly acidic, so it dissolves limestone as it seeps through the rock. When the water reaches the air of a cave, it gives off carbon dioxide and deposits calcium carbonate.
Each drop leaves a thin ring of calcite. The rings build up into a hollow tube called a soda straw, which can later grow into a cone.
A stalagmite is the matching formation that rises from the cave floor where the drops land. When a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, they form a column.
Most stalactites grow very slowly, often a fraction of a millimetre a year. Similar formations can grow much faster from concrete, for example under bridges and in tunnels.
Speleothems, mainly stalagmites, can be dated, and the chemistry of their layers records past climate. Scientists use them to study changes in rainfall and temperature over thousands of years.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: caverns, icicle shape, stalagmites, columns.

alignments.label: Stone icicles in caves

britannica.quote: stony bodies hanging from the roofs and sides of caverns, in the form of icicles

wikipedia.quote: a mineral formation that hangs from the ceiling of a cave

alignments.note: The description holds. Only the words changed.

alignments.label: Drops leave stone behind

britannica.quote: the water, dropping slowly, leaves these particles behind, which harden into stone

alignments.note: A change in language. Calcareous earth is the old name for lime, which is calcium carbonate.

alignments.label: How water takes up stone

britannica.quote: carries with it particles of calcareous earth or spar

wikipedia.quote: it dissolves limestone as it seeps through the rock

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. The water carries the lime dissolved, not as particles. The role of carbon dioxide is not in the 1797 entry.

alignments.label: Stalagmites from the floor

britannica.quote: raise up stony cones or pillars called stalagmites

wikipedia.quote: rises from the cave floor where the drops land

alignments.note: The same fact in both texts.

alignments.label: Joined into columns

britannica.quote: these, meeting with the stalactites from above, often form entire columns

wikipedia.quote: When a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, they form a column

alignments.note: The same fact and nearly the same words.

alignments.label: A vegetation of stone

britannica.quote: a kind of vegetation of stone, which grows from a seed like a plant

alignments.note: Stalactites are not alive and have no seed. The 1797 entry gives this as the view of older writers, not as its own.

alignments.label: Quick growth

britannica.quote: closed up by them in a few years

wikipedia.quote: Most stalactites grow very slowly, often a fraction of a millimetre a year

alignments.note: Growth is usually very slow. Inference: the 1797 report may describe a cave with unusual water, or it may exaggerate.

alignments.label: Famous caves

britannica.quote: the grotto of Antiparos in the Archipelago, and of Pool's Hole in Derbyshire

alignments.note: Both caves are real and known for their formations. The Wikipedia passages do not name single caves.

alignments.label: Records of past climate

wikipedia.quote: the chemistry of their layers records past climate

alignments.note: New knowledge. Dating methods for cave deposits came long after 1797.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1797 entry explain how stalactites form?
Do stalactites grow as fast as the 1797 entry said?
Did people think stalactites were alive?

How did the 1797 entry explain how stala.answer: Water filters through the rock, carries particles of calcareous earth, and leaves them behind as it drops [B2]. Wikipedia agrees on the dripping water but says the water dissolves the limestone and then deposits calcium carbonate when it gives off carbon dioxide in the cave [W2].

Do stalactites grow as fast as the 1797.answer: Usually not. The entry said some close a passage in a few years [B5]. Wikipedia says most grow a fraction of a millimetre a year, though similar formations on concrete grow much faster [W5].

Did people think stalactites were alive?.answer: Some older naturalists did. The 1797 entry reports that they saw stalactites as a vegetation of stone that grows from a seed [B4]. Wikipedia describes a stalactite as a mineral formation [W1], built from calcium carbonate left by water [W2].
